1: Welcome to the story deck for Building Provider Notices, a developer workbook in the Federal Modernization Workbook.
Instead of eight chapters one at a time, we'll follow one notice all the way through: an Azure Service Health retirement of basic public IP addresses, action required by September 30, 2027.
It's fictional: every value comes from the kit's own test fixtures, and every output on a slide is what the kit really printed.
The workbook is a draft, awaiting the owner's review.
And the code is illustrative, tested against fixtures, not against a lyve tenant.
2: Scene one: Azure Service Health reports the retirement, and the kit makes it one record.
Scenes two to five ask the same question of Microsoft 365 in G C C, Oracle Cloud, AWS and Google Cloud: how does each provider say something needs action, and by when?
Those scenes use each provider's own fixture notices, because our retirement is Azure's.
Scene six gives the notice an owner, as a Ticket-to-Machine task.
Scene seven carries it into the weekly digest and the evidence chain.
And scene eight deploys the whole loop, test first, then production.
Each scene has a story slide, a try-it slide with real output, and a one-question check.
3: Microsoft Learn's Resource Graph samples for Service Health show a retirement as a health advisory with the subtype retirement.
Nothing in the event says action is required.
So the kit does three things.
It merges the event's rows from every subscription into one notice.
It applies a stated rule: a retirement is action required, due at the advisory's end.
And it writes who said so, the kit's rule, not Microsoft.
Then it fingerprints the record, so reading it again next week changes nothing.
Why it matters: monitoring the provider, and receiving its advisories, with evidence the security officer can keep.
4: From the kit's folder, collect Azure from the day-one fixtures.
Five notices, all valid against the schema, two needing action.
Five from six rows, because one incident's rows from two subscriptions became one notice.
Read the records, and there's our retirement: open, action required, due September 30, 2027.
The window runs a year, the due date is the window's end, and the action basis says rule, Azure retirement, due at the advisory end time.
The source link is the event on the commercial Resource Manager host, and the fingerprint is the record's hash.

Scene three, Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, where an agency's H R platform may well run.
Oracle's documentation gives the announcement a type, and that type can itself be action required.
That's Oracle's own flag, so no kit rule is needed.
The fixtures' example is a change: replace the certificate bundle on load balancers, due December 15, 2026.
The kit reads the latest announcement in each chain, so a rescheduled window replaces the first.
And it knows Oracle's realms: commercial, and the U S Government realm with its own regions.

AWS's documentation says AWS Health tells each account which of its instances will be retired, and when.
AWS has its own actionability field, and when it says action required, that's the provider's word.
But a scheduled change that names a retirement or lifecycle event without that flag could look optional, so the kit makes it action required by its own rule, due at its start.
Two things to know: the Health A P I needs a qualifying support plan, and the GovCloud partition has a single endpoint.
The kit names the partition, and checks the caller is in it.
13: First, the partitions: commercial AWS in its Health region, and GovCloud in its single West region, each with its own ARN prefix.
Then, after collecting the fixtures, read each notice's action basis.
The EC2 instance retirement and the security notification say provider, actionability action required: AWS said so.
The Lambda planned lifecycle event says rule: a scheduled change whose event type names a retirement, due at its start.
Maintenance and the closed incident need no action.
It's the same split our Azure retirement showed: who said it is always written down.

Scene six brings us back to our retirement.
The router matches it against the agency's routing file, rules in order, first match wins.
It becomes a typed task: priority three, assigned to the cloud platform engineering group, with a contingency review, because a retirement that names the agency's resources is a plan change.
Two dates stay apart: the agency's response window, a day, and Microsoft's action date, next September.
The task follows the Ticket-to-Machine pattern from the book Governance, Drift and Evidence: a human-decision lane and five clauses, from origin to the evidence kept.
19: After routing the day-one collection, read our retirement's payload.
Create, de-duplication key azure and the tracking I D, P3 with a twenty-four-hour window, response due the next day, action due September 30, 2027.
Cloud Platform Engineering, contingency review true, and the controls and indicators the step supports.
Then the five clauses: the human decision lane, the notice as origin, the system owner as approver, plan the change under change control, a re-read check, and the evidence kept.
Finally, route the same collection again on a copy of the state.
20: Next spring, Microsoft stops listing our retirement notice.
What does the router do with its task: resolve it, delete it, send an update asking for the re-read, or wait for the action date?
21: The answer to check six: an update asking for the re-read.
A provider closing its notice isn't the agency's work being done.
The digest is for the people who act, and the evidence is for the people who check.
Both come from the same runs, so neither can drift from what was actually read.
Every week, our retirement sits in the digest's action-required section, soonest due first, with the group it was routed to.
And every run is recorded as evidence: its steps, the controls and indicators they support, every file's hash, and the hash of the record before it.
Change a recorded file, and the check fails.
22: After a week of runs, write the digest for the second week and read it.
Under action required, our row: due 2027-09-30, Azure, retirement, routed to Cloud Platform Engineering, with its notice I D.
Then, with the collection, the routing and the digest each recorded, check the evidence: twenty-five files match their sums, three records, chain unbroken.
Now append one line to the recorded digest and check again.
The sums fail on that file, the chain fails on its record, and the check exits with a failure.

Routing runs as a dry run, then a smoke test, then the one write to a cloud, the Service Health alert policy Microsoft Learn describes, applied only with its approved hash.

Now the stage check that failed in the last scene passes on every row, because the pre-flight and the run are recorded.
The Azure step on the test fixture shows one retirement, ours.

Does it pass anyway, fail on the check that reads the test evidence, warn and let the operator decide, or apply the alert policy regardless?
27: The answer to check eight: the pre-flight's last check fails, because production needs the test stage's evidence to pass first.

That's our retirement, end to end: read with the least privilege, made one record that says who decided it needs action, routed to an owner with two dates kept apart, carried in the weekly digest, recorded as evidence the security officer can check, and deployed test first.
Each provider chapter has a second lab in your own test subscription, tenant, tenancy, account or project, and routing has one in a ServiceNow developer instance, never production.
